paras: The attempted lynching of Kay Woods took place in downtown Indianapolis, Indiana, on the morning of August 12, 1903, when a crowd of white men chased and shot at Woods, a Black man, after he and a white man, James Saunders, had exchanged pistol shots. Woods was wounded in the arm, and a patrolman named Dugan held off the crowd with a drawn revolver until other police arrived. Papers outside Indiana carried the story under headlines such as "Small Race Riot in Indianapolis" and "Lynching Is Prevented by Officer With a Gun," and the Indianapolis Journal praised the officer in an editorial.

The quarrel began at about half past six in the morning in a saloon, which the Rock Island Argus placed at West and Washington streets. According to a special dispatch to the New York Herald, Saunders, a night watchman, told a drinking companion that recent race riots had "served the niggers right," and Woods rushed at him. The wire story of August 12 gave a different cause, an argument "over how much education a negro should have."

In the Herald's account the two men struggled out into the street, drew revolvers and emptied them at each other, five shots apiece, hitting Saunders in the hand and Woods in the arm. As Woods ran, a crowd took up the chase, put at "a score of white men" in the wire story and at two hundred by the Argus.

The pursuers shouted "Lynch him," or in the Herald's version "Lynch the nigger!" According to the wire and the Argus, men in the crowd fired at the fleeing man, and a bullet broke his right arm just as he ran into a policeman. The Herald wrote that several men had seized Woods when Policeman Dugan came to his aid with a drawn revolver and kept the crowd back until bicycle policemen arrived. Woods was then taken to the station, with the crowd following "with angry demonstrations nearly to the jail doors."

Police held both Woods and Saunders, and the early reports said both men would recover. The coverage does not report charges, a hearing or a trial for either man, or any arrest of members of the crowd. On August 13 the Indianapolis Journal blamed the "shooting affray" on "the pistol habit" and said Patrolman Dugan deserved credit for facing a mob pursuing a "fugitive negro" with "the usual cry of 'lynch him.'" The editorial added: "Better a dozen persons killed by an officer in the discharge of duty than one lynched."

The story first ran as a short wire item on August 12, which the Washington Times headed "Small Race Riot in Indianapolis" and the Alexandria Gazette printed among its "Telegraphic Brevities." The Beatrice Daily Express in Nebraska ran its own special under the headline "Negro Shot Down," with a subhead stating that Woods had "Killed James Saunders," a claim its text did not make and other reports contradicted. The New York Herald's dispatch of August 13, "Race Duel in a Street," was the fullest account and the only one to report Saunders's remark about the race riots.

A separate dispatch dated August 14 appeared in the Rock Island Argus as "Lynching Is Prevented by Officer With a Gun" and in Indiana's Plymouth Tribune on August 20 under the heading "'Lynch Him!' Of Course." Condensed versions of the wire kept running in news digests through late August, in South Carolina papers under the heading "The Indiana Way," in Wisconsin's Vernon County Censor as "Negro Shot by Indiana Mob," and in the Chicago Citizen. These briefs opened with Wood shooting Sanders, named no one in the crowd, and said nothing of the remark that the Herald reported had started the fight.

The accounts disagreed on how Woods was wounded: in the wire version Wood shot Sanders and was then shot by the mob, while the Herald described a mutual duel in which Woods was hit and mentioned no shooting by the crowd. The Argus reported a pistol fight in which Saunders was hit, followed by a shot from the crowd that broke Woods's arm. The papers also gave Saunders's first name as James in most reports and John in the Argus.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Kay Woods
bases: After a two-way pistol fight with a white man, Woods was pursued, fired on and wounded by a crowd of white men crying 'lynch him' and was saved by a policeman; no one was killed (A2, A5, A6).

The wire (A2, A3), the New York Herald's special (A5), a separate later dispatch (A6) and the local Indianapolis Journal (A4) agree that a crowd pursued Woods crying 'lynch him' and that an officer held it off, though they differ on details.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal praised the patrolman who faced the mob and wrote, 'Better a dozen persons killed by an officer in the discharge of duty than one lynched.'
The wire ran as brief items headed 'Small Race Riot in Indianapolis', 'The Indiana Way' and 'Negro Shot by Indiana Mob', opening with Wood shooting Sanders.
The New York Herald's 'Race Duel in a Street' gave the white man's provoking remark and credited the policeman with saving Woods's life.
The Argus headline 'Lynching Is Prevented by Officer With a Gun' and the Plymouth Tribune's '"Lynch Him!" Of Course' treated the cry as routine while crediting the officer.
